droidSdk.sdkExample:
import asyncio, sys
from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel
from droid_sdk import run

class Triage(BaseModel):
    summary: str
    severity: Literal["low", "medium", "high"]

bug_report = open(sys.argv[1]).read()
result = asyncio.run(run(f"Triage this bug report: {bug_report}", output=Triage))
if not result.success:
    raise SystemExit(result.subtype)
queue = "Priority" if result.output.severity == "high" else "Standard"
print(queue, result.output.summary)

An automation runs a prompt on a trigger with no code to own, while an SDK script lets your code check Droid’s answer and decide what happens next, such as where a bug is routed. Reach for the SDK when a rule must hold on every run.

action.text: Change the routing so medium and high severity go to Priority; low stays Standard. Keep the prompt to Droid unchanged. Rerun the script, test the rule with all three severities, and show the new output next to the first run.

customizeSdkWorkflow.summary: Change the rule, keep the prompt
customizeSdkWorkflow.tip: Keeping rules in code means a change takes one edit and behaves the same on every run. Here, sending medium severity to Priority is one line in the routing code, while the prompt that judges severity stays untouched. Put judgment in the prompt and fixed rules in code; mixing them makes runs hard to compare.

failures.label: Check it ran

judgment.label: Droid judges

rule.label: Code decides

learnDroidSdk.instructions: Read what the script is for, then tap each pin to see what Droid decides and what your code decides.
learnDroidSdk.summary: See where Droid ends and code begins
learnDroidSdk.tip: Reading the script shows where Droid’s judgment ends and your rules begin. In Python, run(prompt, output=Triage) returns a result whose output matches your Pydantic model, and result.success and result.subtype tell you whether the run worked. The TypeScript SDK works the same way, with run() and an outputFormat JSON schema.

The draft asks Droid to show the command, its exit status and the real output, and a failed run reports result.success as false with result.subtype saying why. Keep your API key in an environment variable, never in chat.

conversations.context: Example request: “@Factory Investigate checkout failures in storefront. Use the error below, identify the cause, and report file references. Do not edit code or post elsewhere.” Start with investigation before authorizing a fix.
conversations.contextNote: A bounded investigation is safer than an ambiguous request to fix everything.
conversations.first: For Slack, invite Factory to the channel and select its mention in a thread. For Teams, install the app in the team and select @Factory from the mention picker.
conversations.practice: Use a training thread to request a read-only investigation, answer one clarification, and check a cited source. Do not post sensitive material to a broader channel.
conversations.review: Read the cited files and distinguish findings from assumptions. Slack DMs use your personal identity and connectors; shared channel requests use the service account. Start a separate conversation for a separate task.
conversations.reviewNote: Follow up in the same conversation to keep the task’s context.
conversations.second: Include the repository, error, expected outcome, and limits. Factory reads earlier thread messages when it has permission, so avoid threads with sensitive material; if it cannot, paste the relevant context.
conversations.third: Reply in the active conversation; teammates can follow up too. In Teams, mention @Factory again. Example: “Check whether an empty cart reaches this path; keep the investigation read-only.”
conversations.tip: Slack and Teams can pass the surrounding thread to Droid when Factory can read it. Keep the request understandable on its own in case that context is unavailable

issues.context: Example: checkout fails for an empty cart. The issue names the storefront repository, reproduction steps, expected behavior, and a regression test. Droid can investigate, implement, and test, then return a PR.
issues.contextNote: Name both the intended change and behavior that must stay unchanged.
issues.first: Write the handoff: fix the empty-cart error; preserve payment behavior; add a regression test; run focused tests; return a PR and test evidence. Include relevant errors and links.
issues.practice: Choose a low-risk training issue. Add acceptance criteria and verification steps, delegate it only when you are ready, and ask for the reproduction and test results before reviewing its PR.
issues.review: If tests were skipped or failed, ask what remains unverified. Stopping a run does not undo edits or PRs. Delegation does not replace your repository’s review requirements.
issues.reviewNote: A summary is not test evidence. Inspect the actual result.
issues.second: In Linear, assign Factory or select @Factory in a comment. In Jira, use Agents → Factory or select @Factory in an issue comment.
issues.third: Read progress in the issue’s agent conversation. Answer questions there and inspect the returned diff and tests before merging. Teammates in your organization can follow up in the same conversation.
issues.tip: Reuse the clear-task pattern from Your first session: outcome, context, constraints, and verification. A self-contained issue reduces clarification and makes review easier
issues.title: Delegate an issue

operations.context: Example: “Every weekday at 09:00 UTC, summarize new TODO comments in this repository and return the result here. Do not edit files or post elsewhere. Say ‘No updates’ when nothing changed; report access failures without guessing.”
operations.contextNote: A recurring prompt must stand alone without someone answering questions.
operations.first: Ask the orchestrator to draft the automation first. Check the repository, timezone, delivery session, identity, compute, and repeat/duplicate rules before approving creation. Creation may start a run immediately.
operations.practice: Create a narrow, private practice automation only after approval. Inspect one run, edit a harmless instruction, rerun, and pause it. If Workstreams are unavailable, use the standalone Automations page.
operations.review: A successful status is not proof of a useful report. Check missing access, empty days, repeated findings, and incorrect destinations. Pause unexpected behavior before changing the instructions and testing again.
operations.reviewNote: Check the first run before trusting the next scheduled one.
operations.second: Select + → Automations in the Workstream’s right pane. Open the automation, select Run now, and inspect Events and the linked run. Verify evidence links and delivery to the intended session.
operations.third: Use Edit for schedule changes and the row menu to pause. Cloud execution can continue after your laptop closes; Remote Control must stay online and Local needs the desktop app running.
operations.tip: Reuse Automations’ source, task, output, and limits checklist. Read the first result and pause a training schedule when you finish
operations.title: Operate a recurring workflow

sdk.context: The Python and TypeScript SDKs expose Droid’s agent capabilities to your application. This TypeScript example summarizes a repository with run(), checks the terminal result, and prints the answer.
sdk.contextNote: The application owns invocation, permissions, and result handling.
sdk.first: Prepare Node.js 18+ and the Droid CLI on PATH. In a separate practice folder, install @factory/droid-sdk and import Node APIs from @factory/droid-sdk/node.
sdk.practice: Help me build a TypeScript repository-summary script in a new practice folder. Check the installed SDK docs and prerequisites. Use secure environment authentication; never request my key in chat. Ask before installs or execution. Show the command, exit status, output, and error handling. Do not post or change repository files.
sdk.review: Review tool permissions before running against real data. A prompt saying ‘read-only’ is not a security boundary; use applicable tool controls and permission handling, and do not approve every request blindly.
sdk.reviewNote: Actual output and exit status prove execution; generated code alone does not.
sdk.second: Supply FACTORY_API_KEY securely through the process environment. Never paste the key into chat or commit it. Set the working directory to the repository you intend to inspect.
sdk.third: Run the script and inspect its command, exit status, and output. Check result.success before using text; catch startup/transport exceptions as well. run() closes its session automatically.
sdk.tip: Use an automation when a trigger and instructions suffice. Use the SDK when your application needs to start Droid and control what happens to its result
sdk.title: Run Droid from your code

sessions.context: createSession() supports follow-up prompts with shared history. The second prompt below asks about tests using the first summary’s context. Each turn is consumed before the next begins.
sessions.contextNote: Later prompts share history; independent calls to run() do not form one conversation.
sessions.first: Create a session with deliberate working-directory and permission settings. A session handles one turn at a time; read its stream through the terminal result.
sessions.practice: Extend the practice script with a follow-up question and safe cleanup. Then ask Droid to propose a structured finding schema and routing tests. Inspect the results before connecting any live destination.
sessions.review: Example rule: validated high-severity findings go to Priority; other findings go to Standard. Test all severities and malformed output. Changing that rule should not require changing Droid’s judgment prompt.
sessions.reviewNote: Droid interprets the input; your validated code enforces the fixed rule.
sessions.second: Check each result for failure. Use finally to await session.close(), including when a turn fails. Missing permission handlers can cause approval requests to be declined.
sessions.third: For programmatic routing, request structured output, validate its shape, then apply rules in code. A successful run alone does not prove structured output is present or valid for your application.
sessions.tip: A persistent session keeps conversation context, not a guarantee of correctness. Keep fixed business rules in code and close sessions even after errors
sessions.title: Keep context and enforce rules

setup.context: Delegation apps send work to Droid. Connectors give Droid tools while it works. Shared requests use the requester’s assigned agent profile (Apps by default): its instructions, plugins, service account, and compute.
setup.contextNote: A personal connector does not install the organization’s delegation app.
setup.first: A Manager or Owner opens Settings → Delegations → Set Up for Org. Authorize the chosen app; its administrator may also need to approve installation.
setup.practice: Help me set up one delegation app. Ask which app and repository, check what is already configured, and guide the authorized setup. Explain any administrator action needed. Never ask for secrets in chat. Ask before changing settings or sending a test request; verify access with a read-only task I approve.
setup.review: If settings are unavailable, ask your administrator for app installation, repository/connector access, and working compute. Then send a small read-only request. Opening Settings is not proof that access works.
setup.reviewNote: Verify access as the identity that will execute the work.
setup.second: Under Agent Profiles, review the profile your delegations use (Apps by default): instructions and plugins, an active service account, Git access to every Environment repository, and the connectors the task needs.
setup.third: Choose Dynamic compute with a Ready Environment, or Persistent compute with service-account-owned computers. Use matching Factory and connected-app account emails.
setup.tip: Installing a delegation app and connecting a personal connector are different steps. Check the identity and machine that will actually run the request
setup.title: Prepare delegation access

steering.context: Two agents investigate the empty-cart error: one traces the API, one checks the UI. The orchestrator records findings and dependencies in shared notes before proposing edits.
steering.contextNote: Independent investigations can run in parallel; dependent edits need an agreed contract.
steering.first: Open Agents to follow progress. When an agent appears under Waiting on you, answer the concrete decision. Tell the orchestrator if the answer changes another agent’s scope.
steering.practice: In an available Workstream, request two read-only investigations with distinct ownership. Ask agents to save findings in Files and have the orchestrator summarize dependencies. Approve execution only after reviewing the scope.
steering.review: When work stalls, ask for the blocker, last evidence, and next safe step. Pause or narrow the task rather than launching duplicate agents. Check the diff and test evidence before accepting results.
steering.reviewNote: Review both individual outputs and the behavior they produce together.
steering.second: Use Files for shared plans and findings. Resolve the API contract before dependent edits. Redirect narrowly: “Preserve the current API; change empty-cart handling only.”
steering.third: Open PRs to inspect changes and checks. Ask for an integrated checkout test and evidence of unchanged payment behavior. Do not infer merge permission from permission to implement.
steering.tip: Parallel work needs explicit ownership and shared decisions. Review the integrated behavior, not only each agent’s individual claim of success
steering.title: Steer agents and review results

Set up the FIS peai-engineering-toolkit on this machine. Ask me before each command that changes anything.

{{macosDownload}}

Reference only: AIEE Runbook 1, {{runbookUrl}}. It needs FIS single sign-on, so you may not be able to open it; follow the steps above.

access.definition: Signing in identifies your account. Permissions determine which items Droid can read. A successful sign-in does not prove access to a private channel or document.

agentReadiness.definition: Agent Readiness answers: what makes this repo difficult for agents? Use /readiness-report to inspect setup, documentation, tests, and other gaps. Find reports under Analytics → Agent Readiness when available.

agentsMd.definition: AGENTS.md supplies durable repo guidance: setup and test commands, conventions, and boundaries. Use /init to draft it when missing; review the result. If one exists, ask for a focused improvement, not a replacement.

autonomy.definition: Autonomy sets the highest-risk work Droid can run without pausing for approval. Higher levels let Droid do more on its own, and you can cycle levels as you work through a task.

connectors.definition: Connectors are Factory-managed connections to supported apps. Use them to read an assigned ticket, find a Slack decision, or consult a shared document.

mcp.definition: MCP (Model Context Protocol) connects additional tools through an MCP server. Use it for a team-approved internal service or a tool not covered by a connector.

skillScope.definition: Personal skills in ~/.factory/skills/ follow you across projects. Project skills in .factory/skills/ travel with the repo. Inspect SKILL.md, supporting files, dependencies, and permissions before importing.

skills.definition: Skills package workflows such as reviewing an API change, updating docs, or preparing a weekly report. Droid can load a matching skill, or you can invoke an available skill with /skill-name.

specMode.definition: Droid researches your task and proposes a plan, called a spec, before it changes any code. While planning it only reads and searches: no file edits, commits, or services. Approve the spec to start building, or keep iterating on it.

wiki.definition: Wiki answers: how does this codebase work? Use it to learn architecture, locate a feature, or onboard to an unfamiliar repo. Open Wiki from the profile menu, or ask /browse-wiki a question.

loginRateLimit.explanation: It needs many tries to cause harm: Medium. Plan a fix.
loginRateLimit.prompt: The login form lets anyone try passwords without a limit.

whyNot.p0: Guessing passwords takes many tries, so it isn’t immediately exploitable.
whyNot.p1: An attack needs time and luck, so the risk is moderate.
whyNot.p3: Password guessing can take over accounts, so it’s more than Low.

openAdmin.explanation: Easy to exploit, serious harm, no login: Critical. Block the merge.
openAdmin.prompt: Anyone on the internet can call a new admin endpoint, no login.

whyNot.p1: High needs some condition, like a login. This needs none.
whyNot.p2: Anyone can do it today, so it’s worse than Medium.
whyNot.p3: Open admin access is serious harm, not a small one.

otherInvoices.explanation: Exploitable with a login and leaks real data: High. Fix it before you merge.
otherInvoices.prompt: A signed-in user can read another customer’s invoices by changing an ID.

whyNot.p0: It needs a login first, so it’s High, not Critical.
whyNot.p2: The attack path is real and the data is sensitive, so it’s High.
whyNot.p3: Leaking customer data is serious harm, not a small one.

body.text: The `search` parameter is pasted into the SQL string. Any signed-in user can search for `' OR 1=1 --` and read every customer’s invoices.

fix.text: Pass `q` as a bound parameter, so the database treats it as text, not SQL.
